title: The bloom of the present
hook: some mornings he sat in his doorway from sunrise to noon, unwilling to trade the moment for work (Walden 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the classics, and the Iliad sitting half-read on Thoreau's table. Your line was the best books first. Did one good page get read, slowly? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-eight.

A summer morning at the pond. Thoreau has had his swim. He sits down in the sunny doorway of his cabin, among the pines and hickories, and he stays there. The sun climbs. Birds sing around him and pass through the house. A wagon rattles on the distant road. He doesn't get up. Not at nine, not at ten. Sunrise to noon, he tells us, on some mornings. Somewhere in Concord, a neighbor is already halfway through the day's work. And Thoreau, in the fourth chapter of Walden, says he couldn't afford to do otherwise.
screen: `A SUNNY DOORWAY.` → `SUNRISE TO NOON.` → `HE COULDN'T AFFORD TO MOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the strange economics. Thoreau writes: "There were times when I could not afford to sacrifice the bloom of the present moment to any work, whether of the head or hands." Could not afford. He uses money language on purpose. The man who just printed the cost of his cabin now says some mornings were too valuable to spend on work. Second, the bloom. A bloom doesn't last. It opens, it's at its best, and then it's gone, whether anyone looks or not. The present moment, he suggests, has a bloom like that, and work of any kind, even good thinking, can trade it away. Third, the margin. Then he adds: "I love a broad margin to my life." A page with wide margins isn't wasteful. It's easier to read. There's room for notes, for breath. He wanted a life laid out like that, with space around the words. He says he grew in those seasons like corn in the night. You don't watch corn grow. It just happens while nothing seems to be happening. Fourth, the honest objection. He knew how this looked. To his neighbors, he says, it would have seemed like idleness. He doesn't argue much. He simply reports that those hours were not time subtracted from his life but added to it. You don't have to agree. But it's worth asking when you last let a moment bloom without trying to use it for anything.
screen: `COULD NOT AFFORD TO WORK.` · `A BLOOM DOESN'T LAST.` · `A BROAD MARGIN.` · `IDLENESS, OR GROWTH?` · then, large: `THE BLOOM OF THE PRESENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a doorway. If you can, sit near a door or a window, somewhere with a little outside in it. If not, wherever you are is fine. Let your hands go still. Don't plan. Don't review. For these two minutes, nothing needs to be used for anything. Let whatever is here, light, a sound, the temperature of the air, simply open in front of you, like something blooming that doesn't need you to do a thing. The bell holds the time.
The bloom of the present. Thoreau's phrase in Walden for the moment at its best, which he would not sacrifice to any work, of head or hands, on certain mornings in his doorway. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: the bloom of the present. Today, find a doorway, a step, a porch or an open window, and give it ten minutes with nothing to do. A small broad margin. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Some readers of Walden keep unhurried time in a doorway, on a porch or by a window, after Thoreau's mornings sitting from sunrise to noon.

notes: Verify both quotations word for word against an 1854 text.

Paraphrases to check: on a summer morning, having taken his accustomed bath, he sat in his sunny doorway from sunrise till noon amid pines, hickories and sumachs, while birds sang around or flitted noiseless through the house, until the noise of some traveller's wagon on the distant highway reminded him of the passage of time; he grew in those seasons like corn in the night; the hours were not time subtracted from his life but so much over and above his usual allowance; to his fellow-townsmen this would have seemed sheer idleness.
'Birds pass through the house' and 'a wagon rattles on the distant road' follow the Sounds passage; confirm.
'Not at nine, not at ten' is illustrative, drawn from 'sunrise till noon'.
